pos: n. (Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, c. 1466–1536, humanist scholar, editor of the first published Greek New Testament in 1516, and Luther's opponent on the freedom of the will)
etymology: Greek erasmios, beloved; Latin desiderius, desired — a doubled name of his own choosing. His Greek text, through Stephanus and Beza, became the basis of the Textus Receptus behind the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Erasmus was the greatest scholar of his age, and the church owes him a real debt. His edition of the Greek New Testament (1516), with a fresh Latin version and notes, put the apostolic text into the hands of every scholar in Europe, and the Reformers translated from it. He wished the ploughman might sing Scripture at his plough. His satires on monks and relic-mongers prepared many minds for reform, and it was said he laid the egg that Luther hatched. But Erasmus stayed in the Roman communion, disliked doctrinal conflict, and in 1524 attacked Luther's teaching on the will in his Diatribe. Luther's reply, The Bondage of the Will (1525), thanked him for going to the heart of the matter. The Scriptures settle it: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil” (Jer 13:23); “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16); and freedom comes from Christ alone: “If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (Joh 8:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines will as that faculty of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action; the faculty which is exercised in deciding, among two or more objects, which we shall embrace or pursue.
webster_full: WILL, n. That faculty of the mind by which we determine either to do or forbear an action.
2. Choice; determination.
3. Command; direction.
4. Pleasure; disposition; inclination.
scriptures: Joh 8:36
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil.
Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Psa 12:6
The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
corruption_summary: Erasmus is the scholar who gave the church the Greek text and then refused its doctrine of grace, and he is the patron of every Christian who prizes learning and peace above truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Erasmus's position on the will was moderate, and that was its appeal: a little ability left in fallen man, a little cooperation with grace, and a plea that such questions not be pressed too hard for the sake of peace. That is precisely the posture of much modern evangelicalism, which assumes the sinner retains a free choice to accept Christ and treats the doctrine of the bondage of the will as an unhelpful extreme. Luther saw that the whole gospel turns on this point: if salvation depends on the will of man, it is not wholly of God.

The recovery is to receive Erasmus's gift and refuse his error. His Greek New Testament stands behind the Authorized Version; his doctrine of the will stands condemned by that same New Testament. The Reformed confess with Scripture that the natural man is dead in sin, and that the Son alone makes free.
roots_summary: Hebrew haphak (H2015), to change, turn; Greek thelo (G2309), to will; eleutheroo (G1659), to make free.
roots_lines: Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to turn, overturn, change; Jeremiah 13:23.
Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, wish; Romans 9:16, Philippians 2:13.
Greek eleutheroo (G1659) — to set free; John 8:32, 36, Romans 6:18.
usage: “If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (Joh 8:36) — the answer to the Diatribe.
“it is not of him that willeth” (Rom 9:16) — the text Erasmus could not get round.
“The words of the LORD are pure words” (Psa 12:6) — the text he edited, better than the man.

pos: n. (Charles the Great, c. 742–814, king of the Franks from 768, crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800; under his name the Caroline Books rejected the image-worship of the Second Council of Nicaea)
etymology: French form of Latin Carolus Magnus, Charles the Great.
biblical_def: Charlemagne united most of western Europe under one crown and, at Rome on Christmas Day 800, received the imperial title from the pope's hands — an act the papacy later cited as proof that it made emperors. His reign revived learning, copied the Scriptures, and reformed the schools. But it also baptized the Saxons at the point of the sword, a conversion by conquest that Scripture never authorises. For the Reformers his name mattered chiefly because of the Caroline Books, written at his court in the 790s, and the Council of Frankfurt (794), which rejected the decree of the Second Council of Nicaea (787) ordering the veneration of images. Calvin cites them against Rome in the Institutes. The law was plain: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4). Charlemagne's court also pressed the filioque into the creed in the West. The psalm addresses every such ruler: “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth” (Psa 2:10); and Christ divides their realm from God's: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines emperor as the sovereign or supreme monarch of an empire; a title of dignity superior to that of king.
webster_full: EMPEROR, n. The sovereign or supreme monarch of an empire; a title of dignity superior to that of king.
2. In general, the title of a monarch who rules over many kingdoms or large territories.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Psa 2:10
Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
Pro 8:15
By me kings reign, and princes decree justice.
corruption_summary: Charlemagne's coronation fused throne and altar into Christendom, and both sides of that fusion — the pope who crowns and the king who converts by the sword — corrupt the Scriptural order.
corruption_paragraphs: The coronation of 800 was later read as proof that the pope held both swords, spiritual and temporal, and gave the temporal to whom he would. The forced baptisms of the Saxons were the opposite corruption: the king making the church an arm of conquest. Both erase the line Christ drew. The magistrate bears the sword for justice; the church bears the Word and the keys. Neither may take the other's weapon.

Yet the Caroline Books show a Christian king's court taking a better part, testing a council's decree by the second commandment and refusing it. The Reformed honour that judgment. Kings reign by God's appointment (Pro 8:15), and they serve Him best when they submit their councils to Scripture rather than to Rome.
roots_summary: Hebrew pesel (H6459), graven image; sakal (H7919), to be wise, act prudently; Greek apodidomi (G591), to render, give back.
roots_lines: Hebrew pesel (H6459) — an idol, graven image; Exodus 20:4, Deuteronomy 4:16.
Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to be prudent, act wisely; Psalm 2:10.
Greek apodidomi (G591) — to give back, render what is due; Matthew 22:21, Romans 13:7.
usage: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — the law the Caroline Books upheld.
“Be wise now therefore, O ye kings” (Psa 2:10) — the charge to every Christian emperor.
“unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21) — the line the coronation blurred.

pos: n. (Hildebrand, c. 1015–1085, Pope Gregory VII from 1073, author of the Dictatus Papae, who humbled the emperor Henry IV at Canossa in 1077)
etymology: Germanic hild, battle, and brand, sword. The Reformers commonly called Gregory VII by his own name.
biblical_def: Hildebrand was the driving mind of the eleventh-century papacy and, as Gregory VII, the boldest claimant of its power. His Dictatus Papae (1075) asserted that the Roman pontiff alone may be called universal, that he alone may use the imperial insignia, that all princes should kiss his feet, that he may depose emperors, and that the Roman church has never erred and never will. In the struggle over investiture he excommunicated Henry IV, and in January 1077 the emperor stood three days in the snow at Canossa before he was absolved. Gregory also enforced clerical celibacy with severity. He fought simony and lay control of bishoprics, and those were real abuses. But his remedy was a throne above all thrones, and Christ had forbidden it: “Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them” (Mat 20:25); “But it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26). Peter himself charged elders not to rule “as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3). The Reformers saw in the claims of the Dictatus the portrait of one “Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God” (2Th 2:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines supremacy as the state of being supreme, or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.
webster_full: SUPREMACY, n. State of being supreme, or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.
2. The papal supremacy, the claim of the pope to supreme authority over the church.
scriptures: But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.
corruption_summary: Hildebrand is remembered as a reformer who freed the church from princes, and the praise conceals that he subjected princes and churches alike to one man.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern histories, including many Protestant ones, present the Gregorian reform as a necessary liberation of the church from feudal lords. The abuses it attacked were real. But the Dictatus Papae did not return the church to Christ's rule through His Word and elders; it made the bishop of Rome the lord of bishops and kings, and the claim of an unerring Roman church stands to this day in Rome's own teaching.

The recovery is the Reformation's answer: the church is freed from worldly lords not by a greater worldly lord but by Christ, its only Head, ruling by Scripture through servants who are examples rather than masters. The liberty of the church and the supremacy of the pope are not the same thing.
roots_summary: Greek katakurieuo (G2634), to exercise dominion, lord it over; diakonos (G1249), minister, servant; huperairomai (G5229), to exalt oneself.
roots_lines: Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to lord it over; Matthew 20:25, 1 Peter 5:3.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant, minister; Matthew 20:26.
Greek huperairomai (G5229) — to lift oneself up above; 2 Thessalonians 2:4, 2 Corinthians 12:7.
usage: “But it shall not be so among you” (Mat 20:26) — Christ's word against the Dictatus Papae.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage” (1Pe 5:3) — the apostle's rule for every elder, Rome's included.
“Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God” (2Th 2:4) — how the Reformers read the claims.

pos: n. (Jacopo Sadoleto, 1477–1547, cardinal and bishop of Carpentras, whose 1539 letter urging Geneva to return to Rome drew Calvin's celebrated Reply to Sadolet)
etymology: Italian Sadoleto, Latinised Sadoletus; the Reformers wrote him as Sadolet.
biblical_def: Sadolet was a learned and gracious humanist, a cardinal of the reforming party at Rome, and a man of real piety. In 1539, while Calvin was in exile at Strasbourg, he wrote to the people of Geneva in courteous Latin, inviting them back to the mother church and warning that they had followed innovators. The Genevan council could find no one to answer, and asked Calvin. In a few days he wrote the Reply to Sadolet, one of the clearest statements of the Reformation's case: that the Reformers had not left the ancient church but returned to it; that justification by faith is the first and keenest subject of controversy; and that the church is known by the Word of God, not by a succession of bishops. Calvin's answer was a model of Peter's charge: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15). Its burden was Paul's: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). And its warrant was the apostle's curse on any other gospel, “though we, or an angel from heaven” should preach it (Gal 1:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reply as that which is said, written or done in answer to what is said or written by another; an answer; a rejoinder.
webster_full: REPLY, n. That which is said, written or done in answer to what is said or written by another; an answer.
2. In law, the plaintiff's answer to the defendant's plea.
scriptures: Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
corruption_summary: Sadolet is the gentle face of Rome's invitation to return, and his letter is the template of every modern appeal to set aside the Reformation for the sake of unity.
corruption_paragraphs: Sadolet did not threaten; he wooed. He spoke of the antiquity and unity of the church, of the danger of trusting private judgment, of the long consent of the fathers. The same appeal is made today in ecumenical documents and in the conversions of evangelicals to Rome and Orthodoxy: come home to the ancient church, leave behind the quarrels of the sixteenth century. It is persuasive because it is courteous and because it names a real longing for the church's unity.

Calvin's answer remains the answer. The question is not which body is older or larger but which teaches the gospel the apostles delivered. Unity bought by surrendering justification by faith alone is not the unity of the church but agreement to abandon it. The faith was “once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and it is to be earnestly contended for, with meekness.
roots_summary: Greek apologia (G627), a defence, answer; epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly; anathema (G331), accursed.
roots_lines: Greek apologia (G627) — a verbal defence, answer; 1 Peter 3:15, Philippians 1:17.
Greek epagonizomai (G1864) — to struggle for, contend earnestly; Jude 3.
Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8–9.
usage: “be ready always to give an answer” (1Pe 3:15) — the spirit of Calvin's Reply.
“by grace are ye saved through faith” (Eph 2:8) — the point Sadolet's letter passed over.
“contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — why Geneva did not return.

pos: n. (Albert Pighius, c. 1490–1542, Dutch Roman Catholic controversialist whose attack on the bondage of the will drew Calvin's treatise of 1543 and whose views on predestination Calvin answered in 1552)
etymology: Latinised from the Dutch Pigge. Born at Kampen; provost of St John's at Utrecht.
biblical_def: Pighius was among the ablest Roman writers against the Reformation. In 1542 he published ten books on free choice and divine grace, aimed chiefly at Calvin's teaching in the 1539 Institutes. Calvin answered the first six in The Bondage and Liberation of the Will (1543), learning as he finished that Pighius had died. He took up the rest years later in his treatise On the Eternal Predestination of God (1552). Pighius argued that a will which cannot choose good is not a will, and that God's grace is offered to all and made effective by man's consent. Calvin replied from Scripture that the fallen will chooses freely, but chooses only sin, until God renews it: “you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1). Christ said, “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44), and Paul that “it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Php 2:13). Election rests on God's purpose, “not of works, but of him that calleth” (Rom 9:11). Pighius also defended Roman tradition and papal authority as rules of faith beside Scripture.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace as favour; good will; kindness; and, in theology, the free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
webster_full: GRACE, n. Favour; good will; kindness; disposition to oblige another.
2. Appropriately, the free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
3. Favourable influence of God; divine influence or the influence of the Spirit, in renewing the heart and restraining from sin.
scriptures: Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Rom 9:11
(For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;)
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Php 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
corruption_summary: Pighius's argument — that a will which cannot choose God is no will at all — is the standard objection to Reformed anthropology, and it is now the unexamined assumption of most of evangelicalism.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection sounds like common sense: freedom means the ability to choose either way, so if man cannot choose God he is not responsible. Calvin's distinction answers it. The fallen will is not forced; it acts according to its nature and wants what it wants. Its bondage is not compulsion from outside but corruption within. That is why it is responsible and why it is helpless at once, and why grace must renew the will rather than merely assist it.

Modern decisionism has taken Pighius's side without knowing his name, preaching as though the sinner's will were neutral and needed only persuasion. The recovery is Calvin's: preach to dead men in the confidence that God quickens the dead, and give Him the glory for every will that comes to Christ.
roots_summary: Greek helkuo (G1670), to draw, drag; energeo (G1754), to work in; ekloge (G1589), election.
roots_lines: Greek helkuo (G1670) — to draw, drag; John 6:44, 12:32.
Greek energeo (G1754) — to be at work in; Philippians 2:13, Ephesians 1:11.
Greek ekloge (G1589) — choice, election; Romans 9:11, 11:5.
usage: “dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) — the state Pighius would not grant.
“except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44) — Calvin's first answer.
“both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Php 2:13) — grace that renews the will itself.

pos: n. (Berengar of Tours, c. 999–1088, master of the school at Tours who denied the conversion of the bread and wine into the substance of Christ's body and was forced to recant in 1059 and 1079)
biblical_def: Berengar taught at Tours that the bread and wine of the Supper remain bread and wine, and are the sign and sacrament of Christ's body and blood, not their substance changed. He appealed to Augustine and to the ninth-century monk Ratramnus. Rome condemned him repeatedly. At a synod in 1059 he was made to sign, under fear of death, a formula declaring that Christ's body is sensibly handled by the hands of the priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful. Calvin quotes that formula in the Institutes as proof of how gross the doctrine had become, noting that even Rome's later glosses were embarrassed by it. Berengar recanted again in 1079, and is said to have repented of his recantations before he died. Christ Himself had given the key: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63). The Supper is a remembrance and a communion, “this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19), in which we “shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26); and the sacrifice is finished, for Christ, “after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sacrament as, in ecclesiastical usage, an outward and visible sign of inward and spiritual grace; a solemn religious ceremony enjoined by Christ.
webster_full: SACRAMENT, n. Among the ancient Romans, an oath taken by soldiers to be true to their general.
2. In ecclesiastical usage, an outward and visible sign of inward and spiritual grace.
3. The eucharist or Lord's supper.
scriptures: And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;
corruption_summary: Berengar's forced recantation shows what the doctrine of transubstantiation required its opponents to say, and it exposes the claim that the doctrine was always the faith of the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome teaches that the substantial change of the elements was the unbroken faith of the ancient church, defined at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215. Berengar's case shows otherwise: in the eleventh century a master of a cathedral school could appeal to Augustine and to earlier writers for a sacramental view, and the opposing view had to be imposed by synods under threat. The formula he was made to sign was so crude that later Roman theologians qualified it.

The Reformed confess with the 1689 Confession that Christ is spiritually present to the faith of the worthy receiver, and that the doctrine of transubstantiation is repugnant to Scripture and to common sense. The recovery is not a bare memorial either, but the Supper as Christ gave it: bread and wine set apart to show His death, through which believers feed on Him by faith, while His body remains in heaven.
roots_summary: Greek anamnesis (G364), remembrance; zoopoieo (G2227), to quicken, make alive; katangello (G2605), to shew, proclaim.
roots_lines: Greek anamnesis (G364) — remembrance, memorial; Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24–25.
Greek zoopoieo (G2227) — to make alive; John 6:63.
Greek katangello (G2605) — to proclaim, shew forth; 1 Corinthians 11:26.
usage: “the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63) — the word Berengar would not unsay in his heart.
“this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19) — the Supper as Christ instituted it.
“one sacrifice for sins for ever” (Heb 10:12) — why no altar repeats it.

pos: n. (Gratian of Bologna, 12th century, compiler of the Concordance of Discordant Canons or Decretum, c. 1140, the foundation of medieval canon law)
etymology: Latin Gratianus, from gratus, pleasing. Not to be confused with the fourth-century emperor of the same name.
biblical_def: Gratian was a teacher at Bologna who gathered into one book thousands of texts — conciliar canons, papal letters, sayings of the fathers — and set them in order, resolving apparent contradictions. His Decretum became the first part of the body of canon law by which the medieval church governed itself, and Calvin cites it constantly in Book IV of the Institutes, often to show that Rome's own law condemns its practice. But the collection also carried forward the forged decretals of the ninth century, which put the claims of later popes into the mouths of early bishops of Rome, and it gave legal form to a church whose laws bound consciences that Christ had freed. Christ had warned of men “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mar 7:7). James set the limit: “There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy” (Jas 4:12). The test of every canon is Isaiah's: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). And the believer's charter is Paul's: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines canon as, in ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign; a decision of matters in religion.
webster_full: CANON, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign.
2. The genuine books of the Holy Scriptures, called the sacred canon.
3. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend.
scriptures: Mar 7:7
Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Jas 4:12
There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
corruption_summary: Gratian made the church's traditions into a legal code, and the code became a second authority beside Scripture that bound the conscience in matters God left free.
corruption_paragraphs: The genius of the Decretum was harmony: discordant canons reconciled into one system. Its effect was to make the church's accumulated rules a body of law with the same claim on obedience as the Word of God, administered by courts and enforced by penalties. Fasts, feasts, marriage impediments and clerical privileges became matters of conscience by legislation. The 1689 Confession answers that God alone is Lord of the conscience and has left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to His Word, or not contained in it.

The danger is not confined to Rome. Every church tends to turn its customs into rules and its rules into tests of faithfulness. The recovery is to hold every tradition to Isaiah's test and to refuse to bind where Christ has not bound.
roots_summary: Greek entalma (G1778), commandment, precept; nomothetes (G3550), lawgiver; Hebrew te'udah (H8584), testimony.
roots_lines: Greek entalma (G1778) — a precept; Mark 7:7, Colossians 2:22.
Greek nomothetes (G3550) — a legislator, lawgiver; James 4:12, the only use.
Hebrew te'udah (H8584) — attestation, testimony; Isaiah 8:16, 20.
usage: “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mar 7:7) — the danger of the Decretum.
“There is one lawgiver” (Jas 4:12) — the limit of all church law.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the test of every canon.

pos: n. (Celestius, fl. 410–431, disciple of Pelagius, condemned at Carthage in 411 and repeatedly afterward for denying original sin)
etymology: Latin Caelestius, heavenly. Often more outspoken than his master.
biblical_def: Celestius was a lawyer who became Pelagius's chief disciple and the bolder spokesman of his teaching. At Carthage in 411 he was charged with propositions that put the issue plainly: that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or not; that Adam's sin injured himself alone and not the human race; that infants are born in the state Adam was in before the fall; and that a man can be without sin if he wills. He was condemned there, and again by African councils in 416 and 418. Pope Zosimus at first declared him orthodox, then reversed himself and condemned him; the Council of Ephesus (431) condemned him finally. Augustine's writings against the Pelagians answered him from Scripture: “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned” (Rom 5:12). David confessed it of his own birth (Psa 51:5), Paul of all mankind, “by nature the children of wrath, even as others” (Eph 2:3), and Job asked the question that settles it: “Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one” (Job 14:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heresy as a fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
webster_full: HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
2. Heresy, in law, is an offense against Christianity, consisting in a denial of some of its essential doctrines.
scriptures: Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
Psa 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Eph 2:3
Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.
Job 14:4
Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one.
corruption_summary: Celestius's propositions are not ancient curiosities; denial that infants inherit sin and that death is the wage of Adam's fall is now standard in liberal theology and common in popular evangelical belief.
corruption_paragraphs: Celestius held that death is natural, that sin is learned by imitation rather than inherited, and that a child begins life innocent. Evolutionary theology now teaches the first as settled science, much modern ethics assumes the second, and the third is the instinct of almost every parent. A Christian who says that babies are born sinners is thought cruel. Celestius would recognise the age as his own.

The recovery is the African church's confession and the 1689 Confession's after it: by Adam's sin all mankind fell, the guilt is imputed and the corrupted nature conveyed to all his posterity, and death came by sin. That doctrine is not the opposite of grace but its foundation, for a race that fell in one man can be raised in one Man.
roots_lines: Greek hamartia (G266) — sin, missing the mark; Romans 5:12.
Greek phusis (G5449) — nature, natural constitution; Ephesians 2:3.
Greek thanatos (G2288) — death; Romans 5:12, 6:23.
usage: “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin” (Rom 5:12) — against Celestius's first proposition.
“by nature the children of wrath” (Eph 2:3) — against the innocent infant.
“Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one” (Job 14:4) — the question he could not answer.

pos: n. (Damasus I, c. 305–384, bishop of Rome from 366, whose contested election cost many lives and who commissioned Jerome's revision of the Latin Bible)
etymology: Greek personal name, perhaps from damazo, to tame, subdue.
biblical_def: Damasus became bishop of Rome in 366 after a disputed election against Ursinus in which the rival parties fought in the streets; the pagan historian Ammianus records that a hundred and thirty-seven bodies were found in one basilica in a single day, and remarks that the prize of the Roman see was worth fighting for, since its holders were enriched by the gifts of matrons and rode in carriages. James had diagnosed such a church: “where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (Jas 3:16). John had met the type in Diotrephes, “who loveth to have the preeminence among them” (3Jn 1:9). Yet Damasus also did one thing for which the Western church remained in his debt: he set Jerome to revise the Latin Gospels from the Greek, the beginning of the Vulgate. He opposed the Arians, and the emperor Theodosius in 380 named the faith of Damasus as the standard of orthodoxy. The Reformed reader learns from him that God can use a compromised man to put Scripture into the people's tongue, for His Word is the true treasure: Ezra's Levites “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense” (Neh 8:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines faction as a party, in political society, combined or acting in union, in opposition to the prince, government or state; a party unscrupulous in its methods.
webster_full: FACTION, n. A party, in political society, combined or acting in union, in opposition to the prince, government or state.
2. Tumult; discord; dissension.
scriptures: Jas 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Damasus is cited by Rome as an early witness to papal primacy; his election is the evidence that the Roman see was already sought for wealth and rank, not received as service.
corruption_paragraphs: Roman apologists point to Damasus's synods, his decretals and the Theodosian edict as signs that the primacy of Rome was recognised in the fourth century. What the edict recognised was his orthodoxy against the Arians, not a jurisdiction over the whole church. And the bloodshed that put him in his chair shows what was already happening to the office: it had become a prize.

The recovery is to judge bishops and their claims by the Scriptures, as Isaiah commands (Isa 8:20), and to honour Damasus for the one thing that has outlived his office — his commission to put the Gospels into a better Latin for the people of the West.
roots_summary: Greek zelos (G2205), envying, zeal; eritheia (G2052), strife, faction; philoproteuo (G5383), to love the preeminence.
roots_lines: Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, envy; James 3:14, 16.
Greek eritheia (G2052) — selfish ambition, faction; James 3:16, Philippians 2:3.
Greek philoproteuo (G5383) — to love to be first; 3 John 9, the only use.
usage: “where envying and strife is, there is confusion” (Jas 3:16) — the election of 366.
“who loveth to have the preeminence among them” (3Jn 1:9) — the spirit that made the see a prize.
“read in the book in the law of God distinctly” (Neh 8:8) — the good Damasus did through Jerome.

pos: n. (Phocas, d. 610, Byzantine emperor 602–610, who seized the throne by murdering Maurice and his sons, and who in 607 recognised the bishop of Rome as head of all the churches)
etymology: Greek Phokas, a personal name. The grant is recorded in the Liber Pontificalis under Boniface III.
biblical_def: Phocas was a centurion who led a mutiny in 602, had the emperor Maurice watch his five sons beheaded before he was killed himself, and ruled by terror until he was overthrown and executed in 610. Gregory the Great at Rome had protested to Maurice against the title ‘universal’ or ‘ecumenical’ bishop claimed by the patriarch of Constantinople, calling it a proud and profane title and the mark of a forerunner of antichrist. Yet he congratulated Phocas on his accession. And it was Phocas who, in 607, decreed at the request of Boniface III that the Roman church should be head of all churches. Calvin marks the irony in the Institutes: the primacy Rome claims by divine right was granted by a parricide, and claimed by the successors of the bishop who had called the title blasphemous. Christ had said, “one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8), and Paul that Christ is “the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18). Solomon described Phocas's court: “If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked” (Pro 29:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines usurpation as the act of seizing or occupying and enjoying the place, power or functions of another, without right.
webster_full: USURPATION, n. The act of seizing or occupying and enjoying the place, power or functions of another without right.
2. Use of power assumed without right.
scriptures: Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked.
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
corruption_summary: Phocas is the inconvenient fact in the history of papal primacy: a title Gregory the Great called antichristian, granted to Rome by a usurper with blood on his hands.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome teaches that the primacy of its bishop rests on Christ's word to Peter and has been acknowledged from the beginning. The record of 607 tells a different story — a political grant, made by an emperor who needed the pope's goodwill, of a title that Rome's own most revered pope had denounced a few years before. Calvin did not need to invent an argument; he needed only to quote Gregory against Boniface.

The recovery is the Reformed doctrine of the headship of Christ. No bishop is universal; no see is the head of all churches; the Lord Jesus is the only Head of the church, and the claim of any man to that place is, in the 1689 Confession's words, without warrant.
roots_summary: Greek kathegetes (G2519), master, guide; kephale (G2776), head; proteuo (G4409), to have the preeminence.
roots_lines: Greek kathegetes (G2519) — a leader, master; Matthew 23:8, 10.
Greek kephale (G2776) — head; Colossians 1:18, Ephesians 1:22.
Greek proteuo (G4409) — to be first, have preeminence; Colossians 1:18, the only use.
usage: “one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8) — against the universal bishop.
“he is the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18) — the title Phocas could not give.
“If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked” (Pro 29:12) — the court that granted it.
